An editorial by six authors summarizes Fillmore et al. (2006) as finding no significant protection in studies that kept former and occasional drinkers out of the abstainer group, describes Mendelian randomization as resembling a randomized trial more closely than traditional observational studies, and cites a genetic study in which drinkers carrying a variant linked to lower consumption had lower cardiovascular risk (Holmes et al., 2014). set.plain: In many large studies, people who drank a little (up to about two drinks a day, under 25 grams of alcohol) died at slightly lower rates than people who did not drink. But in most of these studies the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill, and people who drank now and then. When people who drank a little were compared with occasional drinkers, or with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference, though the few studies that made the strictest comparison cannot rule out a small gain or a small loss. Allowing for differences between the studies also shrank the gap. These studies cannot show whether a little alcohol itself helps, harms or makes no difference to how long people live, and researchers disagree.

evidence_set: The minimum of the DALY-weighted curve over all attributable outcomes (the theoretical minimum risk exposure level) was zero standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 drinks a day; the abstract prints the interval per week), and the weighted risk rose monotonically with intake; the protective associations for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes in females were offset by cancers, whose risk rose monotonically with intake. Weights were each outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016, both sexes; curves were fitted for 0 to 12.5 standard drinks a day; a covariate for former drinkers in the reference group was kept only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes. In a sensitivity analysis of the weights, the curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.

Citing a systematic review of Mendelian randomization studies (van de Luitgaarden et al., 2021), the discussion reports that 67% of such studies of cardiovascular disease and 75% of those of diabetes found no association with alcohol, and that only five of 24 tested a non-linear relationship. Stated limitations: drinking patterns not modelled; alcohol use disorders excluded from the TMREL; possible residual confounding, selection bias, measurement bias and reverse causation in the relative risks; self-reported intake; weights that include DALYs caused by alcohol; depression, anxiety and dementia not included, which would possibly lower the TMREL and NDE. Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL on average by 0.058 (0.00 to 0.30), 0.092 (0.00 to 0.50) and 0.146 (0.00 to 0.60) standard drinks a day in three scenarios. Funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

set.plain: Two world models by one research team added up the risks of 22 or 23 diseases and injuries linked to alcohol, each counted by how much illness it causes. For people aged 15 to 39, the overall risk was lowest at no alcohol or almost none, and it was back at a non-drinker's level by about a quarter of a 10-gram drink a day for men and half a drink for women. For people aged 40 and over, the newer model put the lowest point at about half to two thirds of a drink a day, because some studies link small amounts to less heart disease, stroke and diabetes; most studies using genes did not find this for heart disease and diabetes. The lowest point is where the model's gains and losses balance for a whole population, not one person's risk, and in the older model the risk of every cancer it looked at rose with drinking. The models did not look at drinking a lot on some days.

set.plain: In 83 studies of people who drink, death rates were lowest in people drinking up to about 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day) and rose above that. Using the researchers' model, 40-year-olds drinking 100 to 200 grams a week could expect about 6 months less life than those drinking up to 100 grams, 200 to 350 grams about 1 to 2 years less, and more than 350 grams about 4 to 5 years less. About half of the people who drank reported more than 100 grams a week. Compared with people who did not drink, the main studies found higher death rates in their groups drinking 45 grams a day or more; at 25 to 44 grams the results were not clear, except in women in one analysis, and the groups were too broad to show where the rise begins. People reported their own drinking, mostly once and often less than they drank; people who drank more also smoked more; and some who cut down because of illness were probably among the lighter drinkers, so the studies cannot show that the extra alcohol itself shortened life.

set.population: Adults in cohort studies published up to 2010, mostly from high-income countries: 84 prospective cohort reports of adults without cardiovascular disease at the start (Ronksley et al.) and 44 cohort and case-control studies that were not required to exclude heart disease at the start (Roerecke & Rehm 2012); the 592 studies behind the GBD 2016 curves; and the China Kadoorie Biobank (men) and UK Biobank cohorts
set.plain: In many long-term studies, people who drank a little (up to about one drink a day) had about a quarter less heart disease than people who did not drink. But the people who did not drink included some who had stopped, perhaps because they were ill. When the comparison was with people who had never drunk, and men, women, deaths and new cases were kept apart, the difference in men's heart deaths was small and could be chance. In a large UK study, allowing for smoking, weight, exercise, diet and health made the difference at moderate drinking no longer clear. The gene studies we read did not find it. So it is not known whether alcohol itself lowers heart risk, and none of these studies says how many people out of 100 the difference would mean.

set.plain: Some people carry genes that make them drink less, or more. Comparing them avoids some of the problems of asking people how much they drink. In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking less went with slightly less heart disease, and genes for drinking more with more. In a large study of Chinese men, genes for drinking more made no clear difference to heart attacks either way. None of the studies we read found that genes for drinking more lowered heart risk. One UK study suggested that risk rises from the first drink, but a different set of genes gave a different answer. Three researchers argue that gene studies can be misled, for example by family background, by heavy drinking days, or by genes that act in other ways; they did not measure how much this matters, and they note that some other Asian gene studies pointed the other way. None of the studies says how many people out of 100 are affected.

evidence_set: Drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects; genetic variants lower all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and those linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Genotype tests lifelong (and parental) rather than adult exposure; given common unhealthy drinking patterns in adolescence and early adulthood, their lower prevalence in young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking starts atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), such analyses may be testing adult binge drinking and possibly also teenage and young-adult binge drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.

set.plain: Two gene studies, both using a large UK study of volunteers, looked at other heart and blood-vessel problems. Genes for drinking more went with more narrowed arteries, mostly in the legs (peripheral artery disease), even after allowing for genes linked to smoking. In one study, links with a swollen main artery in the belly (aortic aneurysm) and with an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) became unclear once genes linked to smoking were allowed for; the other study found a link with an irregular heartbeat. For heart failure, the two studies disagreed. For blood clots in the veins, no clear link was found, but the study could not rule one out. Some of these results rest on few cases, and neither study gave numbers out of 100.
